Well, we stacked two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers, and they transform under these conjugate representations of the rotation group. I mean, like p-plus and p-minus orbitals, you know?

Hmm, so it's kind of like the Kane-Mele model then?

Yeah, it looks similar, but here's the thing — it doesn't actually host stable gapless surface states.

Wait, really? But does it show any topological responses?

Oh yeah, definitely! We see quantized fractional charge that's bound to these rotational defects — disclinations, right? And there's this pumping of angular momentum when you thread an elementary magnetic flux through it. It's all described by this mutual Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and, well, an effective gauge field for the rotation symmetry.

Okay, and what about Wannier representations?

Right, so the filled bands don't admit a symmetric Wannier representation. But — and this is important — when you add appropriate atomic orbitals, that obstruction goes away. So it's what we call fragile topology.

Which means?

I mean, you can represent the response as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and negative integer coefficients, you know?

Hmm. Does this apply more broadly?

Oh yes! So after analyzing this model as a prototypical example, we showed that all TCIs protected by point group symmetries without protected surface states are either atomic insulators or fragile phases. Remarkably, gapless surface states exist in free electron systems if and only if there's a stable Wannier obstruction.

And then?

Well, we used dimensional reduction to map the 2D problem to a zero-dimensional one, which gave us the complete non-interacting classification and how interactions reduce it.
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243:
So, um, we've got this new AI thing we're calling the Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate, right? DSNS for short. Basically, what it does is, well, it takes different features from objects in all sorts of areas, you know, like chess problems, classical music, famous paintings, that kind of stuff.

Yeah, and then it mixes them together to create new features that can be used to make, I mean, novel things that people might actually find creative and valuable in any of those original areas.

Right, so it's like passing some of the creative work from humans over to machines, you know?

Hmm, okay, so how did you test it?

Well, we tried it out with chess problem composition. We used it to automatically create tons of chess problems by taking attributes from chess problems and tournament games that humans played, and also from famous paintings, computer-generated abstract art, photos of people, and classical music pieces.

Oh, interesting! And how did you know if they were any good?

Well, we assessed the quality automatically using this existing chess aesthetics model that's been validated through experiments. But we also had human experts in chess look at them too.

Right, right. And what did you find?

The results show that, you know, attributes gathered and mixed from chess and other areas using DSNS can actually generate chess problems with pretty high aesthetic quality. Oh, and here's something really surprising—a low quality chess source, like tournament games between weak players, combined with actual photographs of people, produced three-move problems that were just as good or even better than ones from high quality sources, I mean published compositions by experts. And more efficiently too!

Hmm, that's weird. Why does information from a completely different domain even work like that?

Yeah, well, that's still an open question for now. But the approach should work, in principle, for any domain where objects have attributes you can represent with real numbers.
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::28a6b262-a893-4fcb-a538-fc9aa5ad:
So, you know that baryon acoustic oscillation peak, right? The BAO thing we see in cosmic matter distribution out to, like, redshift 3.5 or so?

Yeah, yeah.

Well, it's basically showing us the continued expansion of that sonic horizon we first spotted in the cosmic microwave background temperature patterns.

Oh, interesting.

Right, and I mean, we can now measure where that BAO peak sits to better than 1% accuracy when we use galaxies, you know? With Ly-alpha forests and quasar clustering, we're getting about 1.4 to 1.6% precision.

Hmm, okay.

So anyway, when you combine this with the Alcock-Paczyński effect—

The AP effect, right?

Exactly. That's the one that comes from how the ratio of angular to spatial size changes with distance for these spherically-symmetric sources, you know?

Oh yeah, I see.

Well, the BAO measurement is considered one of the most powerful tools we have for assessing the Universe's geometry.

Makes sense.

So in this paper, we used five BAO peak measurements from the final Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV release. Average redshifts were 0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48, and 2.33.

Wow, okay.

And we did a direct head-to-head comparison between Lambda-CDM—the standard model—and one of its main competitors, the R_h=ct universe.

Hmm, interesting approach.

Right, so we also used a volume-averaged distance probe that assumes constant comoving distance scale r_d, you know, for completeness. Both probes don't depend on uncertain parameters like the Hubble constant, so they're ideal for model selection.

And what did you find?

Well, based solely on the AP effect, R_h=ct was favored with about 75% likelihood versus 25% for the standard model. But with the volume-averaged distance probe, Planck-Lambda-CDM was favored—about 80% versus 20%.

Oh wow.

Yeah, and the joint analysis? Inconclusive. Both models got comparable likelihoods. So we can't really confirm that BAO data alone support an accelerating Universe.
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::efafda31-a3f3-48d6-9d8f-b2b5d4b1:
So, you know, filaments are basically everywhere in the Galaxy, right? And well, they're where stars form, so I mean, being able to detect them reliably is really key to understanding how star formation actually works.

Oh, okay, so what are you trying to do?

Well, we're exploring whether supervised machine learning can identify these filamentary structures across the whole Galactic plane.

Hmm, interesting. So how did you do it?

Right, so we used two versions of these UNet-based networks for image segmentation. I mean, we took H2 column density images of the Galactic plane—you know, obtained with Herschel Hi-GAL data—as our input. Then we trained the UNet networks with skeletons of filaments, like the spine plus branches, that we extracted from these images. Oh, and we also produced background and missing data masks. We tested eight different training scenarios to figure out the best one for classifying pixels as filaments.

And what did you find?

Well, the training lets us create this new image of the Galactic plane by segmentation where pixels belonging to filamentary structures are identified. With this new method, we actually classify way more pixels as belonging to filaments—I mean, more by a factor of two to seven, depending on the threshold we use—than the spine plus branches structures we started with. New structures are revealed too, which are mainly these low-contrast filaments that weren't detected before. We used standard metrics to evaluate the different training scenarios, right? This shows the method is robust and helps us determine an optimal threshold that maximizes recovery of the input labelled pixel classification.

So what's the takeaway?

Well, this proof-of-concept shows that supervised machine learning can reveal filamentary structures throughout the Galactic plane. Detecting these structures, including low-density and low-contrast ones never seen before, offers really important perspectives for studying these filaments.
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::f4961832-eeb4-41fc-8a64-82c30107:
So, look, I mean, let me just say right off the bat that I really do like Cowboy Bebop, you know? Like, the animation and the designs, they're just sublime, right? And oh man, the soundtrack is fantastic, and the action is great too. I mean, when all three of those things come together, well, the show can occasionally become this jaw dropping audiovisual masterpiece, you know what I mean? Particularly in that breathtaking finale.

Yeah, but—

But here's the thing, there are so many problems with it that, I mean, I cannot in good faith call it a "masterpiece" or, you know, proclaim it to be one of the best of the medium. Well, unless we're talking about it as a gateway show, right?

Okay, so what's the issue?

Well, I'll start off with the characters, which is where, hmm, many of my problems lie. I'll admit, Spike and Jet are great characters, but they are only two out of five of the entire Bebop Crew, you know?

Right, right.

So Ein's introduction as a "data dog" or otherwise hyperintelligent canine, it just goes nowhere and he spends the rest of the show just being the crew's pet, which is—

Oh, that's disappointing.

Yeah! And Faye, oh man, Faye exhibits so many of the worst characteristics that can be written about a female character. She's bossy, greedy, obsessed with her own beauty, you know? She needs to either be rescued or she's a hinderance to the group more often than an asset. And she often wears revealing clothing for the sole purpose of fanservice, I mean—

Hmm, yeah.

Ed is hit or miss, and walks the line between endearing and annoying, but hardly receives much development beyond her introductory episode, right? But the main villain Vicious, oh, he is especially bad. He has very little character and motivation aside from a desire for more power, and even though the show goes a bit into his backstory it never establishes motivation, you know?

So at the end of the show—

At the end of the show, Vicious is little more than an evil guy in a black coat with enough fighting skill that it makes Spike struggle to land a bullet in him. Well, aside from the obvious fact that Vicious becomes a representation of the syndicate Spike ran away from, right?

Right.

So as a result the five episodes that involve him, like Sympathy for the Devil, Jupiter Jazz parts one and two, and Real Folk Blues parts one and two, they don't leave me feeling as if they are as spectacular as the show wants me to feel like they are, you know?

Hmm.

And aside from that, well, the quality of the episodes varies dramatically. For an episodic show that only has about five episodes that build an overall story, that's saying a lot, right? I mean, sure, there are fantastic episodes such as Waltz for Venus and Ganymede Elegy, but there are also fairly ho hum episodes such as Bohemian Rhapsody, Speak Like a Child, and Boogie Woogie Feng Shui.

So what do you want?

Well, I mean, help me appreciate this show and tell me what I'm missing, you know?

So, you know, I live in New Zealand, right, and we're like, we're currently in the middle of what they're calling "one of the most important elections in our country's history," apparently, and I'm not planning to vote, and I think—

Oh really?

Yeah, and I think that these campaigns that the electoral commission are running to encourage everyone to vote are just stupid, you know?

Hmm, but why though?

Well, I mean, a lot of the political-minded people around me, right, they don't seem to understand that some people simply don't have a view. Like, when Helen Clark's government ended and John Key came in, did it really affect me? I mean, not really. Actually, not at all.

Right, right.

So if Labour win this year, will it affect me? I don't really think so, you know? I'll continue doing what I do and people will continue to hate the government until, like, a couple of terms later National come back in, and it still has no real effect on my daily life whatsoever.

Okay, so—

So, therefore, I'm of the opinion that I really don't give a shit, and it's not worth my time researching to try and give a shit, therefore I should leave the voting to people who know somewhat what they're talking about, right?

I mean, sure, but—

And that's fine, and it's a generally accepted attitude here, but recently there has been a whole lot of guilting people into voting, you know, with campaigns with slogans like "It's only democracy if you vote, idiot," and I've even seen some extreme ones with a picture of the earth decaying, something about climate change, and just a huge block letter "VOTE" next to it.

Oh wow.

Yeah! And if I were to mention I wasn't planning on voting to half of my friends, they'd be fine with it, but the other half would fucking grill me alive, saying that I'm "not contributing to my country's future," you know?

Hmm, yeah.

Really?

Yeah! Oh, and the green party also came in and offered free bus passes outside of peak hours for uni students, which is like the most moronic policy in the universe, because it achieves nothing in the real world, but it gets a bunch of voters converted, you know?

I mean—

I'm sure the right wing is doing it too, but the left is more apparent to me as a uni student, obviously. So in conclusion, well, people should not be encouraged to vote, they should be encouraged not to vote, if they do not know what they're talking about. People will vote for all the wrong reasons and politics becomes open to extreme manipulation of voters, right?

Okay, but—

The only reason the electoral commission is guilting people into voting is because they are all interested in politics, and don't realise that a lot of people just quite simply don't care. It's like forcing the entire country to watch the rugby, and honestly, the All Blacks losing would have a bigger effect on me than a change in government, you know what I mean? That's just how it is for some of us, right? We're not all political people, and that should be okay, shouldn't it?

"Okay, so, um, I have to be honest here — I'm actually undecided on this whole thing, right? But I'm gonna start by arguing against gay marriage for, well, two reasons basically. First, you know, I lean less towards that side and it seems way more fragile and unpopular, so like, advocating for the weaker position that I feel less strongly about? That helps me practice my argument skills, I mean, you know what I mean? And second, I think — and I'll explain this — the burden of proof is on the side that's for gay marriage, so that's why I started on the other side."

"Hmm, okay, go on."

"Right, so first, there's this video — it's only two minutes — and because of that argument, I feel like the burden of proof is on people who want to redefine what marriage means. I don't have a problem with redefinition itself, but, well, you need a compelling reason to redefine something, right?"

"Sure, yeah."

"So when people answer 'Do you think gay marriage is a good idea?' with 'Why not?' — that's really just the teapot fallacy, you know? They're trying to shift the burden of proof."

"Oh, I see what you're saying."

"And I don't think equality is a good argument here. I mean, it's true that people with different sexual orientations deserve equal rights to life, liberty, freedom, pursuit of happiness — all that stuff in the constitution. But the whole equality thing? It's a red herring in this case."

"Wait, how so?"

"Well, marriage isn't a privilege or a right that has to be equal for all types of relationships. Marriage is an institution built around procreation, right? And homosexual relationships, which can be loving and committed, by definition are non-procreational."

"But what about—"

"Yeah, yeah, I know — there are heterosexual marriages that are non-procreational too, like old couples or infertile couples. But if you watch that video, you'll understand why it's not the same thing. Just because there are exceptions to the norm doesn't mean you can extend the definition to a non-norm, because norms aren't defined by their exceptions, you know?"

"Hmm, okay."

"This 'equality' isn't the same as women voting or black people being free. And, oh, another thing — people present the criteria as 'If two people love each other, why shouldn't they be able to get married?' But marriage criteria have nothing to do with love, or even romantic love."

"Really?"

"Yeah! I mean, if your criteria are two individuals who have romantic or sexual love, then incest is fair game, right?"

"Oh, well, but incest is different because—"

"Because of power issues and genetic defects? Well, there can be power issues in any relationship — heterosexual, homosexual, or incestuous. There's no reason to base marriage legislation on that. And incestuous couples don't have to have children, they can adopt, or they might be infertile or even homosexual themselves."

"So you're saying—"

"Someone could argue that incest should be a valid form of marriage just like homosexuality. You can try to argue against that if you want, but you need valid reasoning because the burden of proof is on you."

"Okay, but—"

"And the 'why would you care?' argument? That's invalid. Just because something doesn't affect anyone badly doesn't mean we can change institutions at whim. Even under utilitarianism, this doesn't work. Gay people can have fulfilling long-term romantic and sexual relationships without calling it marriage, right? Redefining marriage for one group's happiness is like — logically, not emotionally — giving in to lobbyist demands so they'll be happier."

"Hmm."

"Most arguments for gay marriage are appeals to emotion or popularity. The term 'gay rights' was designed to make it sound like we have internment camps for them! Even 'homophobe' was coined to stigmatize the opposition. Just because this issue is popular now, and many opponents are religious fundamentalists using straw man arguments, doesn't make the 'more reasonable side' correct. I mean, if there was a movement to legalize incestuous marriage and it was popular, with videos and websites glorifying those couples, most people would support that too. Why is one sexual deviation — and I mean that with complete respect, no stigma at all — more 'marriageable' than another?"

"Well, you know what? My view actually changed. To be fair though, I was already like seventy-five percent there when I started this whole thing."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::bd4df89c-701f-407b-9fc6-2c51aa5b:
So like, I'm talking about this kind of condemnation that you hear all the time from, you know, certain users on rpolitics, right, and certain OWS members, and oh, that Gawker writer Hamilton Nolan, you know? It's basically this viewpoint, and I mean, I'll paraphrase it roughly here, but it goes something like: the mere fact that we live in a system where some people can amass vastly more money than others is, well, it's immoral in itself, right? And if you do amass wealth under this system, hmm, you're quite arguably a bad person, you know?

Yeah, exactly. Like, hedge fund managers are sitting around spending tens of millions on embalmed sharks and—

Right, right, and don't they know that a tiny fraction of their daily earnings would make a huge difference in other people's lives? I mean, it would be enough to pay off the average redditor's student loans, for example.

Oh totally. Every time I've heard this shitty argument though, I've heard it from activists or internet commenters who hail from, well, the middle-class tier, or maybe working-class tier, of an advanced Western economy.

Hmm, okay, but here's the thing though—

You too have vastly more resources than most people worldwide, right?

Well, yeah, I mean—

Like, if you could save a hundred bucks by not upgrading your smartphone, or by walking home in the rain instead of taking a cab, or eating lentils or beans for a few weeks, or by foregoing that new item of clothing you wanted, you know, you could donate that hundred dollars to save the lives of dozens of kids who would otherwise die of malaria.

Right, so is your comfort, your convenience and entertainment more important than other people's lives?

I mean—

And btw, I will not tolerate deflections to the effect of, oh, "but charities might not use the money responsibly," or "charitable donations could have negative effects on local industry in the long run." You know? As a premise of this CMV, we must stipulate that if wealth could be redistributed, that redistribution would, indeed, benefit the recipients, okay? We must further stipulate that if the average American wanted to donate in a genuinely beneficial manner towards a worthy cause, well, he'd be able to do so. I don't think these are crazy assumptions to make, right?

Yeah, so your view is—

So my view is that people who rail against "the rich," purely on the ground that they're rich, are hypocrites for overlooking their own relative economic standing in the world. If they believe others' wealth should be redistributed to curb inequality, they are hypocrites for not redistributing their own wealth to curb inequality, you know?

Hmm, okay.

Now, I don't donate much to charity, but nor do I regard people richer than me as innately evil human beings. I can acknowledge the preference revealed by my decision-making, which is: I'd rather upgrade to business class than save five hundred lives in a developing country, right? For this reason, if some billionaire would rather upgrade his yacht than dissolve all his assets to promote communism, well, I don't really blame him.

Right, but it seems quite a few people disagree with you?

Yeah, exactly, so I'm curious to see if anyone can change my view here, you know?

"Ah, I see."

"Yeah, and when Migos left to perform at the Hanner Fieldhouse arena, investigators were like, perfect opportunity, you know? So they searched the buses."

"What'd they find?"

"Multiple guns, marijuana, and some other drug they didn't say what it was."

"Geez."

"I mean, officials said the discoveries were intensely concerning because, well, it's a university-sponsored event with over a thousand students there."

"Right, that makes sense. So what are they being charged with?"

"Um, drug possession, possession of firearms in a school safety zone, and possession of firearms during commission of a crime."

"That's serious stuff. Do they have lawyers?"

"Wasn't known on Monday if they had attorneys yet. The Associated Press tried calling and emailing their management team but didn't hear back."

"Were they the only ones arrested?"

"No! About a dozen other people got taken into custody too — all occupants from the two vans."

"Oh wow."

"Yeah, but there's no information yet about what charges those people face."

"Hmm. Weren't Migos pretty big? I mean, they had some hits, right?"

"Oh yeah! They're best known for Versace from 2013 and Fight Night from 2014. They formed back in 2009."

"And this was during what, some special concert?"

"Yeah, the school's annual spring concert. Migos had actually contracted with Georgia Southern to perform there."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::49a2d576-81e8-4b16-889d-beb4a986:
"Oh man, did you hear about that teenager in the Bronx?"

"Hmm, no, what happened?"

"Well, so this seventeen-year-old kid, Hakeem Kuta, right, he died after falling off a roof. Six stories."

"What? Oh my god, that's terrible!"

"Yeah, I know. So basically what happened was, um, police were responding to complaints about some kids smoking weed and hanging around in a building lobby, you know?"

"Right, okay."

"So Hakeem and like five other teenagers, they ran when the cops showed up. I mean, they just bolted up the stairs to the roof."

"Oh jeez."

"Yeah, and the thing is, he was a junior at Bronx Envision Academy. Anyway, so the cops chased them up there, right? And when the officers got to the roof, well, some of the teens jumped over to another roof and got away."

"Uh huh."

"But Hakeem and this fourteen-year-old kid with him, they got trapped by this dividing wall, you know? They were pinned in."

"Oh no."

"So then, I mean, Hakeem jumped over this three-foot wall, but here's the thing—he didn't realize there was this gap between the buildings."

"Oh god, really?"

"Yeah, yeah. And his friend, the fourteen-year-old, he tried to help him. He was holding onto Hakeem's jacket, desperately trying to keep him from falling. The kid was dangling like sixty feet above an alleyway."

"Jesus, that's—"

"I know, right? And then this officer, um, Edmundo Rivera, he grabbed onto the friend to stop him from going over the edge too. But the friend, he lost his grip on Hakeem and, well, he fell. Six stories down to the pavement."

"Oh my god, that's horrible."

"Yeah, so the police ran down to where he fell in the courtyard, and they took him to St. Barnabas Hospital. He was in critical condition on life support."

"Did he—"

"He died Saturday morning, around eleven. This happened Thursday night, so yeah."

"That's so sad. I mean, was he in trouble or something?"

"Well, that's the thing. His father, Munir—he's forty-two, immigrant from Ghana—he said his son stayed out of trouble, doesn't do drugs."

"Really?"

"Yeah, he said, you know, 'It's not so easy. He was a nice kid.'"

"Hmm."

"And get this—the authorities said there probably wouldn't have been any arrests anyway. They just wanted the kids to stop smoking marijuana."

"Seriously?"

"Yeah, I mean, no summonses were issued. They did recover marijuana in the lobby, but still."

"So he died running from something that wasn't even—"

"Exactly. Just trying to get them to leave, you know? The building was on Valentine Avenue in Mott Haven."

"Man, that's just tragic. Over nothing, really."

"I know, right? Seventeen years old. His whole life ahead of him."

"Yeah. God, that's awful."

"It really is."

style_dialogue_interjections.coling::6d5e183d-832b-4aa4-a6e2-563f2423:
"Oh man, did you hear about that Chinese policewoman who fought off some guy with a machete?"

"Wait, what? With her bare hands?"

"Yeah, I mean, she was completely unarmed! Her name's Cao Yu, she's only 22 years old, you know?"

"That's insane. Where did this happen?"

"Well, it was in Guizhou province, right, in southwestern China. Happened earlier this month in some public square."

"So what exactly went down?"

"Okay, so she was on patrol, right, and she sees this guy in his twenties waving around a machete. Actually, he had two knives."

"Oh my god."

"I know! So she confronts him, and he stabs her in the shoulder. The whole thing lasted like five minutes."

"Five minutes? That's forever when someone's attacking you!"

"Right? And get this — the machete was 60 centimeters long. Huge knife. She kept fighting him off even after getting stabbed, and she got more wounds on both her hands before her colleagues finally showed up."

"Jesus. Is she okay?"

"Well, she's in the hospital recovering now. They found her bleeding all over, you know. But she said something pretty amazing."

"What'd she say?"

"She said, 'I couldn't just let the man hurt innocent people.' Can you believe that?"

"Wow. That's incredible."

"Yeah, and she told the local TV station, I mean, she was trying to take the machete from him and stall him until backup arrived. She said there were lots of tourists walking around the square and she needed to make sure they were safe."

"So what was this guy doing anyway?"

"Apparently he'd robbed someone, and that's when Ms Cao spotted him."

"Hmm. What happened when the other cops got there?"

"Well, one of them, this guy Jiao Chun, he said they told the guy to drop the machete but he wouldn't. He kept saying he wanted to rob someone for more money."

"That's messed up."

"Oh, and the story got even bigger when CCTV footage came out this week. Chinese social media went crazy for her."

"I bet!"

"Yeah, on Weibo — you know, their version of Twitter — people were calling her a real tough girl. One person posted something like, 'Those who say they're tough every day aren't tough at all!'"

"Ha! That's true though."

"But someone else asked a good question, actually. They were like, 'Where are the qualified policemen? Why didn't they send an armed, well-trained officer to deal with this guy?'"

"Right, that does seem weird. Why send an unarmed young woman?"

"Exactly. Makes you wonder if they're just too shorthanded or what."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::23d0bd02-f2a0-4752-971c-cac75280:
Person1: Hey Rocky! You know, you've been sitting around all night, man. I mean, get out there and dance with someone, like, oh, that woman over there.

Person2: No way! She looks like the intellectual type, you know?

Person1: Oh come on! What kind of woman do you like anyway?

Person2: Well, I want a woman who's affectionate and, you know, fulfills my every need, right? And that woman over there is just not the right type for me.

Person1: Hey, wait. Where have you been? I mean, times are changing, and you're never going to find a woman who'll shine your shoes and pick up after you all the time, man. Wake up already.

Person2: Oh really? Well, I meet a lot of women like that, but, you know, not at this party. Oh, and I also prefer a woman who'll stay home, cook, clean, and watch the kids, right?

Person1: Okay, but what are your household responsibilities once you get home from work, hmm?

Person2: Hmm. Well, eat, watch TV, and throw out the garbage.

Person1: Wait, wait, wait. I can't believe I'm hearing this, man. In fact, you're never going to get married, you know? I recently read a news report that said 40 percent of women don't think their husbands do their share around the house, and you seem to be that type, right?

Person2: Well, that's the way I am, but what's YOUR idea of the perfect woman then?

Person1: Well, I like a woman who's outgoing, caring, and non-judgmental about people's differences, you know? And it bothers me when people think they're the center of the universe, I mean, like someone I know.

Person2: Well, that's nice for you, but that doesn't change my point of view. I guess I'll have to go home to a TV dinner and my dog, Rusty.

Person1: Hey, and if I stick with you, this is going to be a long, lonely night, man. Say hello to Rusty for me.
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::65648d18-be4d-475d-bcab-2fbcdb8a:
"Hey, so like, there's really two different questions here, you know?"

"Oh yeah? What do you mean?"

"Well, okay, so first the bridge thing. I mean, the Atlantic is really really big, right? Like depending on where you cross it could be even bigger than the whole USA."

"Wow, okay."

"And on top of that, um, it's wet obviously and it gets these crazy storms which can cause quite a bit of damage to concrete and steel, you know, the stuff you'd use to make the bridge."

"Right, right."

"So the ocean is too deep to sink the pilings down to anchor the bridge properly. And it's too stormy and full of waves so a pontoon type bridge would just shake itself to pieces."

"Hmm, makes sense."

"Oh, and it's also big and empty and very few people would really want to drive across it because, I mean, it would be so boring and they wouldn't be able to carry enough fuel for the whole trip anyway."

"Yeah, I guess—"

"I mean the adult version is we can't sink piling to stabilize the bridge and current structural materials won't stand up to the stresses of a pontoon bridge. Maintenance would be an absolute nightmare due to the corrosion from salt water and air. You could only refuel on the crossing if fuel were shipped out to the middle of the ocean, which basically defeats the purpose, right?"

"Oh wow, yeah. What about a tunnel then?"

"Well, okay, so the Atlantic is very very deep. All of that water on top of the ocean floor means there's lots of pressure at the bottom. Kind of like how your ears hurt when you dive deeply at the pool but multiply it by ten thousand."

"Ouch."

"Right? So all of that pressure means if they tried to dig a tunnel it would have to absolutely never ever spring a leak or the walls would crumble down and everyone would drown."

"That's terrifying."

"Oh, and on top of that you'd need really really big fans to make sure there was enough air for everyone down there. You would also have the same problem with fuel."

"Hmm."

"I mean, the real problem would be at the joins of the pre-fabricated tunnel sections which would go into the tunnel hole. There's no way they'd be able to be made strong enough to withstand the pressure and even small leaks at that pressure would penetrate materials like a movie laser."

"Oh geez."

"And on top of that, ventilation of the tunnel would be an enormous issue. You would have thousands of kilometers of dead air that would have to be circulated somehow or you'd never make it through. As above, fuel as well."

"So basically nope?"

"Nope. The ocean is too vast, too deep, and too rough."

"Wait, I found something here online. Is the tunnel possible? Maybe?"

"Well, I guess you could call it just as possible as early nineteenth century engineers thought space travel was, you know?"

"Oh, I see."

"In other words, if enough scientists and politicians get hellbent on making this, it'll be made. Otherwise, very much doubt it."

"Right. Hey, ask yourself these questions though. Why would anyone want to drive all the way across the Atlantic?"

"Yeah, what benefit would a bridge or tunnel even have?"

"Exactly. Who would pay for the construction and how would they get a return on their investment? Who would also be responsible for maintaining it?"

"Hmm, good point."

"Remember this would be in international waters so what country or municipality would be responsible for the utilities and infrastructure?"

"Oh wow, yeah."

"Not feasible, not practical, not necessary."

"Oh, I haven't seen anyone else point this out but you would need to deal with the Mid Atlantic Ridge."

"What's that?"

"Well, the Atlantic Ocean is pulling itself apart at a rate of two point five centimeters a year. So you'll need to deal with volcanoes and earthquakes."

"Oh man."

"Even if someone manages to build a tunnel, would it be practical? Think about how far your car can travel before filling up or how many hours can you drive before getting too tired. If something happens in the middle of the tunnel, it would be hours before emergency personnel reaches there."

"True."

"I mean, absolutely it is possible, even with present technology. It's nowhere near economically viable however, since the cost would be absurdly high and the benefit minimal. The project becomes much more feasible with the technological developments foreseen over the coming decades though."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::6ea6d618-d59e-455d-a265-490e1418:
"Hey, so you know how programs crash sometimes? Well, there are like, oh, so many reasons why that happens. Let me tell you about some of the common ones, okay?"

"Yeah, sure, go ahead."

"Alright, so first there's division by zero. You remember from, I mean, way back in kindergarten math, right? You can't divide a number by zero?"

"Oh right, yeah."

"Well, the result is undefined. So if a program tells the computer to divide something by zero, the computer's gonna tell the program, hey, you're doing something wrong here. And if the program can't handle that situation, well, it may just crash."

"Hmm, okay, makes sense."

"Then there's access violation. So basically, a program is only allowed to access certain parts of memory, you know? Other parts are like, off-limits."

"Right, right."

"So if a program tries to access part of memory that's off-limits, the computer will tell the program that it's doing something wrong. And again, if the program can't handle that situation, it may crash."

"Got it."

"Oh, and then there's deadlock. Let me explain this one. So let's say you and your friend Billy are playing with blocks, okay? You have the red block, and Billy has the blue block."

"Okay..."

"You want to switch blocks, so you tell Billy that you'll give him the red block after he gives you the blue block. But Billy tells you that he'll give you the blue block after you give him the red block."

"Oh no, I see where this is going."

"Yeah! Both of you will just sit there forever waiting for the other person to hand over their block, and you'll never get anything done. That's a deadlock situation, and when it happens inside a program, well, the program freezes up and there's nothing you can do except kill it and start it again."

"Wow, that's frustrating."

"I know, right? And then there's unhandled exception. Sometimes a program will have this special sort of error checking built into it, you know?"

"Uh-huh."

"When an error is detected, part of the program throws an exception, and another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with it. But if an exception gets thrown and is not caught by any part of the program, then usually a dialog will pop up letting you know that, hmm, a problem was not dealt with properly, and the program will terminate."

"Right, I've seen those pop-ups."

"Yeah! So all of these situations are caused by bugs in the program. Bugs are just parts of the program that aren't written correctly, or don't account for every possible thing that can happen."

"Makes sense. But why do some programs have more bugs than others?"

"Well, maybe because the people who wrote the program were in more of a rush or didn't test it as well as they should have, you know? Or because the program is so complicated that it's difficult to deal with every possible situation that might happen."

"Oh, I get it now."

"Yeah, it's like, the more complex something is, the more things can go wrong with it, right?"

"Exactly, yeah."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::37e384a6-d2b8-444e-ac7f-d4288c17:
"So, you know, sometimes if there aren't that many athletes to fill up a whole race in one category, well, they'll run similar categories together. I mean, the less affected cerebral palsy athletes can ride with the less affected amputee riders, right, but they're only scored in their own class. Oh, they do this at most bike races for, you know, speeding things up and consolidating things."

"Right, right. So the Paralympics have a somewhat complicated system, hmm, of classifications and adjustments to try to keep things as fair as possible, you know?"

"Yeah, but unfortunately there aren't a lot of disabled athletes, and well, there's a wide variety of disabilities that confer different advantages and disadvantages."

"Oh, like what do you mean?"

"Well, for example, in wheelchair sports, amputees often have an advantage over those who are merely paralyzed because, you know, they're lighter and more maneuverable."

"Hmm, I see."

"So in the interest of having enough people to hold a competition, I mean, sometimes they just have to accept some disability types will have an advantage. This isn't really any different than the regular Olympics, right? Like, tall people have an advantage in basketball and no one's trying to fix that."

"Right, that makes sense. So how do they decide the categories?"

"Oh, well, the categories are based on what the disability causes, not necessarily the type of disability. If you look at cycling, the categories are people with upper body disabilities, people with one limb disability that can pedal with both legs, people with a leg injury where they only pedal with one leg, and people with both legs affected."

"So if CP affects the legs—"

"Yeah, they'd be put in the last category, just like someone else with another disability that affects both legs. Oh, and the athletes must be internationally classified, which requires an examination of how the disability affects the athlete. This helps ensure people can't game the system."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::5895f991-9d37-49fe-9f39-eeff324a:
"So yeah, they don't always just, you know, play dead. I mean, they also secrete these foul smelling liquids that, like, suggest the meat inside has already decayed, right?"

"Oh really?"

"Yeah! So not all predators can actually eat decayed meat, you know, so it gets left alone as the predator searches for safer food to eat."

"Hmm, that makes sense."

"Well, they also lack theory of mind, so it doesn't occur to them that something could be trying to trick them."

"Right, right."

"I would assume that an animal that even gives off the slightest signal of being sick will be avoided by predators, you know, as this could in turn sicken and potentially be the demise of the predator."

"Oh for sure."

"The animal playing dead may seem like a trivial display, but the predator has to weigh up the risks of possibly ingesting bacteria, viruses, whatever."

"Yeah, I mean, imagine you were defending yourself against someone and your adrenaline got all pumped up and you went batshit crazy at it to defend yourself, right?"

"Uh huh."

"At the point when they stop moving, well, the crisis is over and you start to feel safe again. Whether that is because they are unconscious, dead, or faking it, doesn't matter."

"Right."

"And you are a thinking, reasoning human being, not an animal acting solely on instinct, you know?"

"Oh yeah, exactly."

"Animals that are prey species will have instincts to protect themselves from being attacked and this includes trampling, headbutting, biting, goring with horns or antlers, whatever."

"Mmm hmm."

"Once the thing stops moving, the instinct to defend itself abates and it loses interest."

"Makes sense."

"Animals that hunt have similar instincts about prey that is running away or moving around, it triggers aggression. When the prey stops moving, it loses interest other than the need to feed if it's hungry."

"Right, so for something like a bear—"

"Exactly! Which will likely display territorial or defensive aggression and lose interest when the crisis is over. But this won't work on something like a pack of wolves, that are likely wanting to eat you."

"Oh god."

"Yeah, when you stop struggling, well, it's time to eat."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::a9b058a8-5ce8-448f-820a-6ffba640:
Hey, so you know how this works? It's because of the camera's field of view, right? The FOV.

Oh yeah, I mean, if you're into first person shooter games or whatever, you probably know about FOV already.

Right, exactly. So like, think about what we can see as a cone, you know, starting at our eye and then expanding out, and well, the FOV is basically the angle between those two boundary lines.

Hmm, okay, I think I get it.

Yeah, so in shooter games, the pros actually expand the FOV to get an advantage because, well, it lets you see more of your surroundings, right?

Oh, that makes sense.

So I googled up this quick example of increasing a game's FOV. The image on the left has the FOV expanded to like 65 degrees compared to the default of 45 degrees on the right, you know?

And you can see more?

Yeah! With the larger FOV you can see more on the left and right sides. But here's the thing, you'll also notice that these two trailer things, they look like they're farther away even though the player is standing in the exact same place.

Wait, why is that?

Well, it's because as you increase the FOV, you also change how the light from distant objects is going to converge on your 2D surface, right? Essentially a larger FOV means that objects seem to decrease in size faster as they get farther away.

Oh, I see.

And the opposite is also true, I mean, if you decrease the FOV then it increases the apparent size of far away objects since they now converge on a larger portion of the view area.

Hmm, okay.

So the camera on DSCOVR that was used to take these pictures has a FOV of just 0.61 degrees. It makes it very effective at collecting light from far away objects because, well, it's focused on a very small cone. It also means that the distance between the Earth and the Moon doesn't have the same effect on relative size as it does when taken with a regular camera or human eyes.

Right, so it's like, hold your hand in front of your face, you know? It's probably about as big as your monitor.

Okay, yeah.

Now keep your hand in the same spot and move your head backwards. Your hand now appears smaller than the monitor, right?

Oh yeah, definitely.

There's a certain distance where your hand and the monitor get smaller together, at the same rate. This is because the distance between you and those two things becomes a lot greater than the distance between those two things.

Hmm, I think I follow.

Angular diameter depends on distance and ratio of distances. Basically, the first image is very close to the moon and far from the earth, so the moon seems big. The second image is very far from both the earth and the moon, so they appear like their actual relative sizes. So yes, the earth does appear smaller in the second image, but the moon got smaller a lot faster, just like your hand.

Oh, that's a good way to explain it.

Yeah, so DSCOVR basically had its camera zoomed in more, you know? The EPIC camera on the spacecraft that took the image is specifically designed to observe the Earth from a distance, whereas the cameras on the Apollo missions were more general purpose.

Right, makes sense.

To be more precise, in a camera the focal length of the lens determines the physical size of the image formed on the sensor. Then the physical size of the sensor determines the field of view, and well, the pixel resolution of the sensor determines the size of each pixel in the image.

Okay.

With analogue film there are no pixels but the film still has a resolution limit because of its chemistry and there's also a resolution limit imposed by the lens. Finally a large image can simply be cropped, although the DSCOVR image is in fact pretty much its full size, you know?
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::1770be09-c92d-43e3-ab15-7b7318ca:
Hey, so um, first off, you know there are like many different kinds of radiation, right? I mean, light is actually radiation too, but you're talking about ionizing radiation, yeah? Like the kind that bombs and power plants use, correct?

Oh, okay, well you're going to need me to explain what an atom is first. So basically, an atom is the basic building block of everything in the world, you know? They're made of protons, neutrons, and electrons. Different numbers or combinations of these things, well, they result in different atoms.

Right, so most atoms are stable. They don't change at all, but hmm, some aren't stable. The ones that aren't stable will actually SEEK stability by offloading protons, neutrons, and electrons over time, you see?

Oh wow, and these particles are sent away very quickly, which is what makes them so dangerous. They're like tiny little bullets that hit other things at the atomic level, you know what I mean?

Yeah, exactly! If they collide with another atom, they hit it with enough force to send that atom's protons, neutrons, and stuff scattering everywhere, like a pool ball hitting a big group of pool balls, right?

So basically what happens is that certain elements are unstable, and to increase their stability, they release particles and energy, which is known as radioactivity. This happens because there are too many particles in the atom for it to be stable, you see?

Oh, it's like a crowded elevator! Since there are so many people, everyone is uncomfortable, and some people will just leave the group instead of sticking together to go all the way to the top, you know?

Right, so eventually enough people will leave, and the elevator will be comfortable again. This is actually how lead is formed. It's uranium that has released enough particles to make it stable, or comfortable enough for the particles to stay together without losing anyone.

Well, radiation is different types of light, ranging from radio waves to X-rays and beyond, you know? Some atoms are radioactive, which means they fall apart, and when they do, energetic bits fly off.

Oh, and one kind of bit that flies off are gamma rays, which is a form of light, and therefore radiation. When scientists first discovered radioactivity, they didn't fully understand the different kinds of light, so there was a lot of confusion over what was radiation, what was radioactivity, and what was both, right?

I mean, that's why some people still use radiation when they mean radioactivity. So, to review: radiation is different kinds of light, radioactivity is bits that fly off of radioactive atoms, and gamma rays are both!
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::3dd39352-d471-4ab9-bd50-b7345fc1:
So yeah, you know what you're asking about? Well, it's called a 'wealth tax', or um, sometimes a 'capital tax'. Right, so these are taxes that aren't based on income you earned in a year, but more like, I mean, some measure of how much you actually own.

Oh really? Like what kind of examples?

Well, some countries — Italy I believe is a prime example — they tax ownership of foreign land. And then, you know, some countries tax amounts owned by corporations. Canada did this until like five or ten years ago depending on the province.

Hmm, interesting.

Yeah, and some countries strictly tax your wealth above a certain level. Switzerland does this, as has been mentioned.

Right, right. So does anything like this exist in the US?

Oh yeah, one form of what you're referring to that does exist in the US is the 'Estate Tax'. This is basically a tax on the amount of wealth that a person owns at the time they die, you know?

Okay, so when does that kick in?

Well, the threshold for when this tax applies has been very volatile over the last twenty years, but it's generally in the multi-millions. I believe it sits somewhere around five million dollars.

Wow, okay. So do you think we'll see more of these?

I mean, if these taxes start to crop up more and more — and I believe they will — don't be shocked at the initial sticker price, right? Theoretically a wealth tax could replace some of the current income tax regime in many countries without creating a strict increased tax burden on their people.

How would that work exactly?

Well, like, if you owe ten thousand in income tax this year, but a two thousand dollar capital tax is instituted next year, then you're still in the same position as long as your income tax is reduced to eight thousand.

Oh, I see what you mean.
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::8eb96c1a-6193-4f0f-843b-4b91efbe:
"Okay, so like, you could have both options exercised and assigned to you on the same day, right? But I don't think you'd actually lose money on both the same day."

"Wait, why not?"

"Well, it's because, you know, exercises happen immediately, but assignments get processed after the markets close at the end of each day. There's this website, um, 888options.com that explains it in their FAQ section."

"Oh, okay."

"So basically, you'd get both assignments at the same time that night. And, I mean, the net effect should be that you don't own any stock anymore—someone would put the stock to you, then it'd get called away, right? And you wouldn't have the options anymore either."

"Hmm, so what about the money?"

"Right, so you should have incoming cash of fifteen hundred dollars from selling the stock to whoever exercised the call, and then outgoing cash of thirteen hundred buying from the put exerciser. You follow?"

"Yeah, I think so."

"So in the morning, you'd have no more options but two hundred dollars more cash in your account. You bought at thirteen and sold at fifteen."

"Oh, I see."

"This options position is basically an agreement to buy at thirteen and sell at fifteen at someone else's option, you know? The way you lose money is if one of the options isn't exercised while the other one is."

"Like how?"

"Well, if the stock's below thirteen, nobody's going to opt to buy from you at fifteen, but they'll sell to you at thirteen. Or if it's above fifteen, nobody's going to opt to sell to you at thirteen, but they'll buy from you at fifteen."

"Right, right."

"You make money if neither gets exercised—you keep the premium you sold for—or if both are exercised, you keep the gap between the two plus the premium. Having both exercised is surely rare though, since early exercise is rare to begin with and tends to happen when options are deep in the money. So having both exercised on the same day can't be common, but it's maybe most likely just before expiration with minimal time value, if the stock moves around quickly."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::59aec439-babf-4d21-b03b-4f331a96:
"So hey, okay, the first thing you gotta do is, um, look at your credit card terms and conditions, right? Or just call your bank and ask them how they're gonna apply your payments."

"Oh, right, yeah."

"Because, I mean, like Dilip said in his answer, you know, in the US they'll probably put the minimum payment toward the lower rate balance, and then—"

"Mmm hmm."

"—well, then they have to put everything above the minimum toward the higher rate balance. But in other countries, you know, it varies by law and custom and stuff."

"Oh, okay."

"So don't just assume it's gonna pay off the higher balance first, or like, proportionally, without asking. You really gotta check."

"Right, right."

"So let's say, um, you owe six thousand dollars. Five thousand is at thirteen point five percent—that's your normal purchase rate—and a thousand is at twenty-two percent, which is the cash advance rate."

"Ugh, yeah."

"Well, if your bank applies payments to both balances proportionally, then a payment of six hundred bucks will reduce your purchase balance by five hundred and your cash advance balance by a hundred."

"Okay, so the average APR then is, what, just the sum of the product of the APR times balance?"

"Exactly! So here it's, hmm, point one three five times five thousand plus point two two five times a thousand, all divided by six thousand, which equals fifteen percent. That's called a weighted average."

"Got it."

"But here's the thing—if the bank applies the payment differently, like to the lower rate first, or some specified part to the lower rate and the rest to the higher rate, then, well, this'll be misleading if you enter it into a calculator."

"Oh."

"Because your average APR will rise over time as you pay off the purchase balance but don't pay off the cash advance balance. Or it may decrease if the opposite happens, you know?"

"Right, yeah."

"The weighted average is probably reasonably close in your situation, even with different rules, so long as they don't pay down the lower rate a hundred percent. So it may be the simplest option for rough calculations."

"One approach using online calculators that might be better is to treat these like two separate loans or cards. Many calculators exist for multiple balances, and then you can allocate funds differently to the two cards. This would let you see how long you'll need until you've paid off the higher balance, although it probably won't perfectly match things unless you find a site with this specific option."
style_dialogue_interjections.coling::9e189795-5152-41d4-9713-20ef5189:
So, um, Wyoming is actually a really good state for this, you know? It's inexpensive and, well, the annual compliance stuff is pretty minimal.

Right, right. I mean, Delaware has the best advertising campaign, so—

Oh yeah, everyone knows about Delaware!

Exactly, but here's the thing — the reality is that there are, like, over 50 states and jurisdictions in the United States, right? And they all have their own competitive incorporation laws to attract investment. Plus, you know, they've all got their own legislative bodies that keep changing those laws.

Hmm, so you just have to—

You just have to read the laws to find a state that's favorable for you. What I mean is, well, whatever Delaware does to get in the news about its easy business laws? That's been mimicked and done even better by other states by this point in time, honestly.

Oh, interesting. What about Delaware's Chancery Court though?

Well, here's the thing — all other states in the union can also lean on Delaware case law, so that perk isn't really unique to Delaware, you know?

Right, right.

So Wyoming is actually cheaper than Delaware for, like, nominal presence in the United States. It requires less information than Delaware, and it's also tax free.

Okay, but how do I—

A registered agent can get you set up! You can find one to help you with the address dilemma. This should only cost like $99 to $200 over the state fees.

Oh, so an LLC doesn't need to have an address in the United States?

No! I mean, many registered agents will let you use their address. Just ask them.

Hmm, what about banking though?

Well, many kinds of businesses still require a bank account for domestic and global trade. But, you know, many don't require any financial intermediary anymore to receive payments. But if you do need this, then opening a bank account in the United States will be more difficult.

Right, so how—

The registered agent or lawyer can get a Tax Identification Number for you from the IRS. You'll need that to open a US bank account. But honestly, it's more likely that you'll need an employee or nominee director in the United States to go in person to a bank.

Oh, to actually open the account?

Yeah, exactly. This person needs to be mentioned in the Operating Agreement or other official form on the incorporation documents. They'll simply walk into a bank with your articles of incorporation and operating agreement showing they're authorized to act on behalf of the entity, and they open a bank account. Then they resign — that's just a private document between the LLC and the employee. But you'll be able to receive and accept payments and access the global financial system now. Look, I really can't stress this enough, you know, so I'm just gonna say it again: Don't plan your finances around your credit score, okay? I mean, don't even think about your credit score at all, right? Just plan a budget and stick to it. Make sure you include short and long term savings in your budget, you know what I mean? Pay your bills on time. Use credit responsibly. Do all of these things, and well, your credit rating will take care of itself, honestly. Don't try to plan your finances around raising it, okay?

Oh, and on the subject of 0% financing specifically, right, my rule of thumb is to only ever use it when I have enough money saved up to buy the thing outright. And even then, you know, only if my budget will still balance with the added cost of repaying the loan. Other people have other rules, I mean, including not taking such loans at all, and you should develop a rule that works for you. But you should have a rule, right? One rule you shouldn't have is, well, "do whatever will optimize your credit score" because, like I said, you shouldn't plan your finances around your credit score.

All things considered, hmm, I think the most important thing in your situation is to make sure that you don't let the teaser rate tempt you into making purchases you wouldn't otherwise make, you know? You're not really getting free money. You're just shifting around the time frame for payment, and only within a limited window at that, right?

Also, oh, be sure to read the fine print in the credit agreement. They can be filled with gotchas and pitfalls, I mean. In particular, if you don't clear the balance by the end of the introductory rate period, well, you can sometimes incur interest charges retroactively to the date of purchase. Make sure you know your terms and conditions cold, okay?

It sounds like you're just getting started, so best of luck, and remember that Rome wasn't built in a day, you know? Patience can be the most effective tool in your personal finance arsenal.

Oh, and by the way? Don't plan your finances around your credit score.

"So, you know, people think that OTC companies aren't serious, but I mean, that's really not true at all."

"Oh really?"

"Yeah, well, a lot of these companies are just starting out there because, you know, they don't meet the requirements for NASDAQ or NYSE yet. I mean, the major exchanges only want the best companies trading on them, right?"

"Hmm, okay, so what are the requirements then?"

"Well, NASDAQ has three different sets of listing requirements. A company has to meet at least one of those sets, plus there are main rules that all companies have to follow. You know what I mean?"

"Right, right. But doesn't OTC have, like, no rules or something?"

"Oh no, that's not true either! I mean, sure, there's no minimum revenue or profits or assets required, but they do have requirements. Companies need audited financial statements and ongoing filing and reporting to the SEC and NASD."

"Oh, I didn't know that."

"Yeah, and there are actually several different levels of OTC too. There's the OTCQX, the OTCCB, and the OTC Pink. Each one has its own requirements, you know. If you want more info you can check out otcmarkets.com."

"Interesting. So what does it cost?"

"Well, when a company decides to trade on OTC, they're making the decision to go public, right? And they're investing to make it happen. Currently the fees range from like thirty thousand to a hundred and fifty thousand dollars."

"Wow, that's—"

"I know! I mean, I wouldn't consider thirty grand to not be serious money, you know what I'm saying?"

"Yeah, absolutely."

"And hmm, when I looked into the TSX process, their requirements seemed more relaxed than the major U.S. markets. It's basically an application, records submission, and then a TSX committee decides if you get listed. You can find more at the TMX website."

"So why does OTC have such a bad reputation then?"

"Oh, well, I think it's from all those 'Get Rich on Penny Stock' companies, you know? They pump up OTC stocks and get massive amounts of people to buy without doing their due diligence or reading the prospectus."

"Right, and then—"

"And then when they lose a bunch of money on an ill-informed decision, they blame it on the company being an OTC stock!"

"That makes sense."

"So whether you trade OTC or not, I mean, I wouldn't make a decision based on how many exchanges the company's listed on. Base it on your research into the company itself, you know?"

So, you know, I just came from the cinema downtown in Prague, right? I saw this film and, well, I mean, it wasn't because of the poster — oh man, that poster looked so old-fashioned Hollywood heroic style, you know what I mean?

Yeah, I get it.

And it wasn't because of all the big stars either because, hmm, well, most of those high-starring French films are usually pretty pathetic, right?

Oh, totally.

But, I mean, there aren't that many films in French — that's my mother tongue — in a city like Prague, so...

Right, right.

Plus I love Adjani and Depardieu and, oh, Rappeneau's Cyrano!

Yeah, that was great!

So anyway, I decided to write this comment because, well, I really don't agree with the mainstream comments on this film on IMDb, you know?

Okay, so what did you think?

Well, I wasn't disappointed, but not in a good way! The film just looks like the poster. The characters are just as stupid as they look. For a while I thought, hmm, maybe Adjani would be like a caricature, you know, a funny character you can laugh at.

But she's not?

No! Like, for example, when she decides to tell Depardieu she's the one who murdered that fat guy she killed at the beginning, right? Then the violins come in with this big fat pathetic music that should make you cry and realize, oh, Adjani's character is deeper than she looks!

Ugh.

I mean, maybe this was humor at the tenth level, but I'm sorry, my sense of humor isn't that high! If I want to see some funny French film about World War II, I'll watch La Grande Vadrouille again — it's way more fun!

Fair enough.

Oh, and people on IMDb say Lemoine gives a great performance. Well, I have to say I've never seen such bad acting! I mean, I've never seen an Ed Wood film, but still! The film is well-filmed though with very costly scenes.

"Oh man, this soap, right, it's worse than bad — I mean, it's actually poisonous, you know?"

"Yeah?"

"Well, like, of all the TV shows that have had this corrosive influence on British society over the past twenty years, Eastenders is the prime example, right?"

"Hmm, go on."

"For two decades this show has celebrated the oaf, the thug, the wide-boy, the tart, the gobby, you know, the violent, the sexually-incontinent, the criminal, the ignorant, the unambitious—"

"Oh, I see what you mean."

"How many times has someone remarked that Eastenders 'mirrors life'? I mean, life on which planet, exactly?"

"Right, right."

"Well, it's written about 'working-class' characters, as imagined by middle-class people who've taken a course in creative writing, you know? They're eager to show to their middle-class peers how familiar they are with the 'working-class,' so they dream up this lumpen rabble that is the citizenry of Eastenders."

"Hmm, that's—"

"And this has a toxic effect on some minds less well-equipped than others to handle fiction, right? So we find members of the real population assuming the attitudes and demeanour of the inhabitants of Walford."

"Oh wow."

"Thus, it came to pass that Eastenders mirrors life, but only after life had been hoodwinked into mirroring Eastenders, you see?"

"Yeah, yeah."

"Other soaps have followed in EE's footsteps, filled to their stinking gunwhales with ugly, potato-faced, shaven-headed, pot-bellied characters, scowling at each other and issuing threats constantly, I mean—"

"That's the proletariat as perceived by the writers who produce this trash, right?"

"Exactly! Well, the writers will grow rich on the proceeds of such output and will go on to enjoy the finer things of life in their rarified enclaves. Meanwhile, the burgeoning number of new, TV-induced drones will proceed inexorably toward cultural bankruptcy."

"So there you have the new priests and the new creatures of the early 21st century?"

"Yeah, much of this is due to the immeasurable power of that illuminated boxful of dancing pixels in the corner of your living-room. It's your fault, gentle reader: that's what you chose as the only window through which to look out from your prison, you know?"

"You know what really bugged me? Like, every single time—"

"Oh, the explorers thing?"

"Yeah! Every time we're about to see one of these amazing new worlds, right, the filmmakers just—I mean, they throw in some emergency or whatever."

"Hmm, a false alarm?"

"Exactly! Some artificial dramatic thing, you know? So instead of just, well, calmly enjoying Io's surface or—"

"Right, or standing over Saturn's rings—"

"Yes! Or concentrating on flying by a comet or an asteroid, we're sitting there worrying about whether the characters are gonna survive. I mean, big let down!"

"So what do you think they wanted? Like, were they—"

"That's the thing! The filmmakers seem totally unsure. Do they want a documentary about the natural wonders in our solar system, or do they want a suspense thriller where we care more about the characters than—"

"Than the actual subject matter?"

"Right! Come on. Hello. If I wanted suspense and tension, I'd just watch a real narrative sci-fi movie, you know?"

"Well, it's a docu-drama though—"

"Sure, sure it's a docu-drama. But the characters and their survival here—I mean, the risks of such a mission—should be secondary to the subject matter."

"Oh, wait though. Aren't the risks an important part—"

"Yes! The risks ARE important since, you know, essentially this is a film about a space mission, not just about the solar system. But it was overplayed and distracted strongly from discovering new worlds we were supposed to be enjoying."

"Hmm. Was anything good about it?"

"Oh yeah! Otherwise, the film was remarkable in giving a very realistic feel for the human elements—the squabbles, the tensions, the weight of responsibility, the near-fatal mistakes, the sacrifices, all that."

"Right, and the science?"

"Well, it would fit very well in hard sci-fi—one of the best, actually, because the science was almost closely adhered to. But those distractions were just awful."

"What else did you miss?"

"Oh! They didn't show the effects of being in space for several years on the astronauts after landing on Earth."

So, okay, this movie stars Ben Kingsley as Frank, right? He's like a hit man working for these Russian mobsters, you know, based out of Buffalo. Oh, and get this — he's also a total raging alcoholic, and I mean, that's really caused his job performance to go downhill.

Yeah, so after he falls asleep in his car during what was supposed to be a hit, well, his mob boss uncle sends him off to San Francisco. He's supposed to attend AA meetings there and, um, get a job as a mortician's assistant.

Right? I mean, if you're thinking that makes absolutely no sense—

Oh, you're definitely not alone there!

Exactly. And it gets worse. Well, actually it gets better, but not before it gets much, much worse first, you know? So Frank suddenly becomes this master mortician even though he has, like, a complete lack of training. But his reactions with the people at the funeral home and the AA meetings? Those are actually interesting.

Hmm, yeah, the viewer starts to root for him because you notice these positive changes happening in his life. Luke Wilson shows up as Frank's sponsor, which is a welcome addition, although honestly he's given almost nothing to do. I mean, his character does tell us he's gay, but that ends up having no significance whatsoever.

Right, so then the movie just plunges headlong into total idiocy with the introduction of the Tea Leoni character.

Oh God, yes. She is completely unrealistic, and her role as a love interest to Frank? It just flounders because the two actors have zero chemistry together.

Exactly. Around the time she comes into the picture, well, Frank becomes much less engrossing as a character. His characterization is seemingly random. There's no consistency in his behavior at all. The comedy is pretty low-key and only intermittently funny, which is especially disappointing considering, you know, the comedic pedigree of the cast.

Yeah, problems abound in this one. Kingsley's accent is terrible and inconsistent. It alternates between Italian, Russian, and Hispanic. Throughout the movie, Frank tells numerous people he's a hit man — including an entire AA group — but nobody seems to care or wants to do anything about it.

The movie relies on cliche scenes to carry it through its final act, most notably when Leoni's insufferable character chases Frank down at the airport just when he's about to board a flight back to Buffalo.

Though it has a strong premise and an interesting first half-hour, the movie quickly becomes a total disaster and devolves into complete nonsense. At the end, Frank celebrates one year of sobriety. I hope to celebrate many, many years of not having seen "You Kill Me." My grade? D.

style_literary.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The capacity to predict with confidence how complex systems will unfold through time stands as a cardinal objective across the scientific disciplines. Yet this ambition encounters formidable obstacles in the realm of modeling: frequently, the governing equations that describe the physics of a given system remain inaccessible to us or, when known, demand computational resources so extravagant that they render timely prediction impossible. Little wonder, then, that the practice of approximating complex systems through generic functional architectures—training these structures from scratch using observational data alone—has flourished in our machine learning era, as the proliferation of triumphant applications built upon deep neural networks abundantly demonstrates. Nevertheless, questions concerning the generalizability of such models, their margins of reliability, and the influence exerted by the character of training data receive insufficient attention, examined primarily through appeals to prior physical understanding rather than systematic investigation. We address these questions from an alternative vantage point by embracing a curriculum learning strategy. In curriculum learning, one structures the dataset so that the training process advances from elementary samples toward increasingly intricate ones, thereby promoting both convergence and generalization. This concept, developed and validated in robotics and control theory, we here apply systematically to the learning of complex dynamical systems. First, drawing upon insights furnished by ergodic theory, we establish the quantity of data sufficient to guarantee in advance a faithful representation of the physical system, and we thoroughly examine how the composition and organization of the training set shapes the quality of long-term predictions. Building upon this foundation, we employ entropy as our metric for dataset complexity. We demonstrate that an informed design of the training set—one guided by entropy analysis—yields substantial improvements in model generalizability, and we offer guidance regarding both the volume and the selection of data necessary for effective data-driven modeling of dynamical phenomena.
style_literary.coling::7876816d-0ac2-4404-b2bf-deeaa0b7: Among the great coolants of the interstellar medium dwelling within galaxies, the CII line at one hundred fifty-eight microns stands paramount, though from one celestial object to another we observe substantial variations whose causes remain obscure. What generates this emission across galactic distances continues to elude our full understanding. Earlier investigations of CII emission in galaxies have achieved resolutions no finer than several kiloparsecs, meaning that the observed radiation represents an average drawn from disparate components of the interstellar medium, their individual contributions blurred together. Our purpose in this work is to examine, for the first time, the CII emission at the intimate scale of a single spiral arm. We seek to trace the origins of this spectral line and to assess its reliability as a marker of star formation. Using the Infrared Space Observatory, we present observations of CII and OI along a segment of a spiral arm in Messier thirty-one. We compare the CII emission with tracers of neutral gas—carbon monoxide and neutral hydrogen—and with tracers of star formation, specifically hydrogen-alpha and Spitzer twenty-four micron emission. The resemblance between the CII emission and both the hydrogen-alpha and twenty-four micron images proves striking when all are smoothed to identical resolution, whereas the correlation with neutral gas appears considerably weaker. The CII cooling rate per hydrogen atom climbs dramatically from approximately two point seven times ten to the minus twenty-six ergs per second per atom at the map's border to roughly one point four times ten to the minus twenty-five ergs per second per atom in regions where stars are forming. The CII to far-infrared ratio, measured between forty-two and one hundred twenty-two microns, holds nearly constant at two percent, a value three times higher than typically quoted. We do not believe, however, that Messier thirty-one is anomalous. Rather, whole-galaxy fluxes used for comparison incorporate central regions where the CII to far-infrared ratio is demonstrably lower, and previous resolved observations neither isolate individual spiral arms nor extend as far into the galactic disk as our present data. A fit to published photodissociation region models yields a plausible average solution of radiation field strength near one hundred and density near three thousand for the photodissociation region emission in the star-forming regions of this arm.
